title: Computational Geometry: From Models To Predicates
notes: Open by making the chapter's promise concrete: computational geometry begins with real spatial situations, but the algorithm never sees a city, robot, or map directly. It sees points, segments, polygons, and predicate answers. The triptych is synthetic, not copied from the book, and lets the instructor ask what modeling decision each application forces before any theorem can be useful.

title: What Counts As A Geometric Algorithm
notes: Use this slide to define the working pipeline for the whole course. An application suggests a geometric object, the object is reduced to a small set of primitives, and the primitives are organized by a data structure. The point is that a geometric algorithm is not only arithmetic on coordinates; it is a representation choice plus a sequence of certified local decisions.

title: Convexity As A Segment Test
notes: Introduce convexity as a universal segment test rather than as a picture of a rounded object. For every pair of points inside the set, the connecting segment must remain inside. This turns a global-looking shape property into a simple inspection question, and it prepares students for why hull algorithms only need to preserve boundary evidence.

title: Hull As A Computable Boundary
notes: Shift from convex sets to the finite output an algorithm can return. The convex hull may be defined as the smallest convex set containing the points, but a program reports a cyclic list of extreme vertices. Emphasize that the clockwise order is part of the answer because later predicates, containment checks, and edge traversals depend on that order.

title: Why The Definition Is Not The Algorithm
notes: Use the contrast between the infinite intersection definition and the finite edge certificate. The mathematical definition explains uniqueness, but it does not say which lines or halfplanes to examine. A hull algorithm succeeds by finding enough boundary witnesses so that every input point is on the allowed side of every reported oriented edge.

title: Slow Convex Hull
notes: Present the slow method as a correctness microscope. For each directed pair of input points, test whether all other points lie on the same side. If they do, that directed pair is a hull edge candidate. There are quadratically many pairs and a linear witness scan for each, giving cubic time, which is too slow but very useful for understanding the certificate.

title: The Orientation Predicate
notes: Make the determinant the first real primitive of the chapter. Its sign says whether the triple turns left, turns right, or is collinear, and its magnitude is twice the signed area of the triangle. This is the bridge from geometry to implementation: the algorithm does not reason with pictures; it branches on this predicate.

title: Degeneracy Is Not A Footnote
notes: Treat collinearity as part of the specification rather than a rare annoyance. When the orientation value is zero, left and right are not valid categories, so the algorithm needs an on-segment or tie-breaking rule. Students should see that degeneracy changes control flow, output conventions, and proof statements, not merely a line of defensive code.

title: When Floating Point Breaks Topology
notes: Explain robustness through topology, not just through numeric error. If nearly collinear triples are classified inconsistently, the directed edge graph can acquire crossings, gaps, or repeated boundary decisions that no polygon could realize. The lesson is that a tiny arithmetic perturbation can become a discrete structural error after predicates drive branching.

title: Incremental Design Move
notes: Now replace the cubic search with a sorted incremental plan. Sorting the points left to right gives a one-dimensional schedule, and the hull boundary splits naturally into an upper chain and a lower chain. The design move is powerful because it limits every update to the current chain end instead of reconsidering every pair of points.

title: Andrew/Graham Scan Stepper
notes: Walk through the stack behavior as an algorithmic state diagram. Append the next point, inspect the last three points, and pop the middle one while the local turn violates the chosen clockwise invariant. Each pop removes a vertex that cannot remain on the final chain once the new point is included, so the state keeps a visible geometric meaning.

title: Handling Equal x And Collinear Runs
notes: Use this slide to pin down output convention. Equal x-coordinates require a secondary order so the scan has a deterministic schedule. Collinear runs require a choice: keep only endpoints for the minimal hull polygon, or keep boundary collinear points for an inclusive boundary listing. Either convention can be correct if the predicate and proof use the same rule.

title: Proof Of Theorem 1.1 As Invariants
notes: Frame the theorem proof as three invariants rather than as a block of text. After processing a prefix of the sorted points, the stored chain is the relevant hull chain for that prefix; the empty slab between consecutive processed points prevents hidden future points from invalidating past interior decisions; and each point is appended once and popped at most once, explaining linear scan work after sorting.

title: Cost Model
notes: Compare the two algorithms on the same axes. The slow method spends work on all directed pairs and all witnesses, leading to cubic growth. The scan pays for sorting and then performs a linear number of stack actions. The point is not just a better asymptotic bound; it is the design pattern of trading global search for an ordered local invariant.

title: Robustness Design Phases
notes: Connect the chapter's robustness discussion to a disciplined workflow. First simplify the problem under a general-position assumption so the idea is visible. Then integrate degeneracies into the formal cases. Finally choose predicate implementations that preserve the combinatorial decisions the proof assumes. This order keeps clarity without pretending that hostile inputs disappear.

title: Where This Book Goes Next
notes: Close with a routing map from the introductory hull story to later computational geometry themes without using Chapter 2 content as substance. The common thread is the same: model a spatial problem, choose primitives, maintain a data structure, and certify local events with predicates. The slide should leave students seeing convex hull as the first example of a broader algorithm design language.
